questions.title: Mathematical Literacy concepts, a strip chart of streets and chair-assembly instructions

subQuestions.questionText:
TABLE 1 below contains a list of explanations and definitions of concepts used in Mathematical Literacy.

**TABLE 1: EXPLANATIONS AND DEFINITIONS OF CONCEPTS**

| Letter | Explanation or definition |
|---|---|
| A | A drawing showing the streets for a person who drives a car |
| B | Visual indication of the real-life distance and its distance on the map |
| C | The boundary that surrounds a circular-shaped object |
| D | A position which roughly shows the location of an object |
| E | The sum of the areas of all the faces of a 3D object |
| F | The rate of covering a certain distance |
| G | The amount of space that is enclosed by the perimeter of an object |

Use TABLE 1 above to write down the letter of the explanation or definition (A to G) of the following concept:

**Bar scale**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **B** — Visual indication of the real-life distance and its distance on the map (2A explanation)
Teaching point: A bar scale is a small ruler printed on a map. It shows you, in picture form, how a length measured on the map compares with the matching real-life distance on the ground.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Scale concepts

Use TABLE 1 above to write down the letter of the explanation or definition (A to G) of the following concept:

**Surface area**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **E** — The sum of the areas of all the faces of a 3D object (2A explanation)
Teaching point: Surface area is the total of ALL the outside faces of a solid. Do not confuse it with option G (area of one flat shape) or with volume (the space inside the solid).

subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **F** — The rate of covering a certain distance (2A explanation)
Teaching point: Speed compares distance with time: $\text{speed} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$. That is why it is described as a *rate* of covering distance.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Speed concept

subQuestions.questionText:
Mr Masunte stays at a guesthouse in Hearn Street. A strip chart shows the streets he will use to reach his destination.

The strip chart is a single line showing his route. It starts at the guesthouse in Hearn Street. Working along the route from the guesthouse, the streets that branch off the route are, in order:

**Fraser → Goring → Aston → Winchester → Oxford → Iffley → Marlow → Regatta → Ewelme → Nuneham → Eyensham → Cleve → Chalgrove → Destination**

Write down how many streets Mr Masunte must cross before turning into Winchester Street.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **3** streets (2A number of streets)
Teaching point: Read the strip chart from the starting point (the guesthouse) and count only the streets that come BEFORE Winchester Street — Fraser, Goring and Aston. Winchester itself is not counted, because he turns into it.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a strip chart

subQuestions.questionText:
Mr Masunte stays at a guesthouse in Hearn Street. A strip chart shows the streets he will use to reach his destination.

Working along the route from the guesthouse, the streets that branch off the route are, in order: Fraser, Goring, Aston, Winchester, Oxford, Iffley, Marlow, Regatta, Ewelme, Nuneham, Eyensham, Cleve and Chalgrove.

The Klip River is drawn on the strip chart as a wide shaded band running across the route between Oxford Street and Marlow Street. The only street drawn crossing over this shaded river band is Iffley.

Name the street that goes over the Klip River.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **Iffley** (2RT correct street read from the strip chart)
Teaching point: On a strip chart, a river is drawn as a shaded band cutting across the route. The street drawn on top of (crossing) that band is the one with the bridge over the river.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a strip chart

subQuestions.questionText:
Mr Masunte stays at a guesthouse in Hearn Street. A strip chart shows his route to his destination.

Distance markers (small circles) are printed along the route. The KEY states that each value indicates the distance between two consecutive markers.

Starting at the guesthouse and moving towards the destination, the marked distances between consecutive markers are:

| Section of route | Distance |
|---|---|
| Guesthouse to 1st marker | 980 m |
| 1st marker to 2nd marker | 435 m |
| 2nd marker to 3rd marker | 870 m |
| 3rd marker to destination | 1 100 m |

Calculate the total distance from the guesthouse to his destination.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Total distance $= 980 \text{ m} + 435 \text{ m} + 870 \text{ m} + 1\,100 \text{ m}$ (1RT first 2 correct values; 1RT second set of values)
Mark 3: $= 3\,385 \text{ m}$ (1CA distance)
Teaching point: On a strip chart the numbers give the distance of each SECTION, not the running total. To get the whole trip you must add all the section distances together.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Total distance

subQuestions.questionText:
The steps and components needed to assemble an office chair are illustrated in the question paper. The components are labelled alphabetically (A–L).

**COMPONENTS NEEDED TO ASSEMBLE THE CHAIR**

| Letter | Component |
|---|---|
| A | Chair back |
| B | Chair seat |
| C | Seat mechanism |
| D | Gas lift |
| E | Chair base |
| F | Chair arms |
| G | Casters |
| H | Screws |
| I | Screws |
| J | Screws |
| K | Washer |
| L | Assembly tool: Allen key |

Each of H, I and J is a picture of a screw, and the three pictures show screws of different lengths and head sizes.

Determine how many different types of screws are needed to assemble the different parts of the chair.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **3** different types of screws (2A number of types of screws)
Teaching point: Read down the component list and count how many separate entries are described as *Screws* — items H, I and J. Each entry is a different type (different length or head), so the answer is 3.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading assembly instructions

subQuestions.label: 1.3.2 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
The question paper shows FIVE assembly drawings (STEP 1 to STEP 5) for an office chair, plus a picture of the completed chair. Letters on each drawing point to the part being fitted.

**STEP 1** shows a five-armed star-shaped stand lying on the floor with a small wheel at the end of each arm. Three labels appear on this drawing:
- **E** points to a cylinder (the gas lift) with an arrow showing it being dropped into the hole in the centre of the stand.
- **F** points to the five-armed star-shaped stand itself.
- **G** points to one of the wheels being pushed into the end of an arm.

(In STEP 2 the labels are A and C; in STEP 3 they are A, B, C, J and K; in STEP 4 they are A, B, D, F and H; in STEP 5 they are A, B and E.)

Use the steps to assemble a chair to identify the following:

The letter that indicates the chair base
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **F** (2A correct letter)
Teaching point: The chair base is the five-armed stand that the wheels (casters) fit into and that the gas lift drops into. On the STEP 1 drawing that stand is labelled **F**. Note that the letters used on the assembly *drawings* are not the same as the letters in the components *list* — always read the label off the drawing the question refers to.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading assembly instructions

subQuestions.label: 1.3.2 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
The question paper shows FIVE assembly drawings (STEP 1 to STEP 5) for an office chair.

**STEP 4** shows the chair turned upside down. The chair seat (labelled A) and the frame of the chair back (labelled B) are in place, and the gas lift is labelled D. Above the underside of the seat, FOUR screws are drawn with dotted arrows showing each one being driven down into a hole in the seat mechanism — three of these screws are labelled F and one is labelled H.

Use the steps to assemble a chair to identify the following:

The number of screws used in step 4
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **4** screws (2A correct number)
Teaching point: Count the individual screws drawn with arrows in that step — not the number of different labels. Four screws are shown being driven in, even though only two different letters (F and H) are used to label them.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading assembly instructions

subQuestions.questionText:
The components needed to assemble an office chair are labelled alphabetically (A–L).

**COMPONENTS NEEDED TO ASSEMBLE THE CHAIR**

| Letter | Component |
|---|---|
| A | Chair back |
| B | Chair seat |
| C | Seat mechanism |
| D | Gas lift |
| E | Chair base |
| F | Chair arms |
| G | Casters |
| H | Screws |
| I | Screws |
| J | Screws |
| K | Washer |
| L | Assembly tool: Allen key |

Name the tool needed to assemble the chair.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **Allen key** (2A correct tool)
Teaching point: Only one item in the list is described as an assembly tool — item L, the Allen key. All the other items are parts of the chair itself.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading assembly instructions

subQuestions.questionText:
The components needed to assemble an office chair are labelled alphabetically (A–L). In the components table each picture shows exactly how many of that item are supplied: every component is drawn as a single item, except for item F, which is drawn as TWO matching mirror-image pieces (a left one and a right one).

**COMPONENTS NEEDED TO ASSEMBLE THE CHAIR**

| Letter | Component |
|---|---|
| A | Chair back |
| B | Chair seat |
| C | Seat mechanism |
| D | Gas lift |
| E | Chair base |
| F | Chair arms |
| G | Casters |
| H | Screws |
| I | Screws |
| J | Screws |
| K | Washer |
| L | Assembly tool: Allen key |

Identify the component of the chair that comes as a pair.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **Chair arms** OR **F** (2A correct item)
Teaching point: A chair has one arm on the left and one on the right, so the arms are supplied as a matching pair (a left-hand and a right-hand piece). This is why item F is drawn as two mirror-image shapes.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading assembly instructions

questions.title: Conference room layout plan, packing bottled water and a road map to the Pretoria Hotel

subQuestions.questionText:
The question paper shows the layout plan of a conference room in the Pretoria Hotel. The plan is a top view of the room and shows the position of the oval conference table, the chairs, the plants, the refreshment table, the screen for presentations, the windows and the door.

Define the term *layout plan*.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: A layout plan describes the physical arrangement of all the structures that consume space within a facility. (2A correct definition)

OR

A layout plan is a top view that shows the arrangement of features / structures / the location or position of items. (2A correct definition)

Teaching point: Two ideas must appear for full marks — that it is a view from ABOVE (a top view), and that it shows where things are PLACED (the arrangement or position of the items in the space).
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Layout plans

subQuestions.questionText:
The layout plan of the conference room in the Pretoria Hotel shows an oval-shaped conference table in the middle of the room, with chair symbols drawn all around the outside of it.

The chairs around the oval-shaped table are drawn as follows:

| Position around the oval table | Number of chair symbols |
|---|---|
| Along the one long side | 7 |
| Along the opposite long side | 7 |
| Around the one rounded end | 3 |
| Around the other rounded end | 3 |

(A separate row of 10 chairs is drawn along the long, narrow refreshment table. Those chairs are NOT around the oval table.)

Write down the total number of chairs around the oval-shaped table.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **20** chairs (2A number of seats)
$7 + 7 + 3 + 3 = 20$
Teaching point: Work around the table in an orderly way (long side, long side, end, end) and count only the chairs that touch the oval table. The chairs at the refreshment table must be left out.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Reading a layout plan

subQuestions.questionText:
The layout plan of the conference room in the Pretoria Hotel shows the following:

- A north arrow. On the plan north is towards the bottom of the page, which means east is to the left of the plan, south is towards the top and west is to the right.
- The screen for presentations is drawn as a long, narrow bar standing against the wall on the RIGHT-hand side of the plan.
- The door leading into the room is drawn (with its swing arc) in the wall on the LEFT-hand side of the plan, directly across the room from the screen.
- The windows are drawn as the long openings in the walls at the top and at the bottom of the plan.

Which ONE of the following statements regarding the conference room layout is TRUE?

A. The screen is on the eastern side of the room.
B. The screen covers some windows.
C. The screen is opposite the door leading into the room.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **C** — The screen is opposite the door leading into the room. (2A correct option)
Teaching point: Statement A is false: north is towards the bottom of the plan, so the right-hand wall (where the screen stands) is the WESTERN wall, not the eastern one. Statement B is false because the windows are in the top and bottom walls, while the screen stands against a side wall. Only C is true — the screen and the door face each other across the room.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Direction and position

subQuestions.questionText:
On the layout plan of the conference room in the Pretoria Hotel, north is towards the bottom of the plan.

The table on the northern side of the room is the long, narrow refreshment table (49 cm wide and 290 cm long), with a row of 10 chairs along it. Three plants are drawn down the middle of the large oval conference table, but NO plants are placed on the narrow refreshment table on the northern side.

Give ONE possible reason why plants are NOT placed on the table on the northern side of the room.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: The north table is narrow / small, so there is too little (limited) space on it. (2O acceptable reason)

OR

Plants would block or obscure the view of the participants seated at that table. (2O acceptable reason)

Teaching point: A reasoning question like this must be answered from the plan itself. The two facts you can see are (i) that table is much narrower than the conference table and (ii) people sit right along it — so either "no space" or "blocks the view" earns the marks.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Interpreting a layout plan

subQuestions.label: 2.1.5 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
The actual outside length of the conference room is 12 m.

Measure the outside length of the conference room on the layout plan.

NOTE: This is a measuring task — in the examination you place a ruler on the printed layout plan and read off the length of the outside wall of the conference room. On the original printed question paper this length measures about 12,7 cm (127 mm). The marking guideline accepts any measurement from 12,4 cm to 12,8 cm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **12,7 cm** or **127 mm** (2A measured value)
Accepted range: 12,4 cm – 12,8 cm (different print runs of the paper measured slightly differently in different provinces).
Teaching point: Line the *zero* mark of your ruler up with the outside edge of the wall, not the end of the ruler, and read to the nearest millimetre. Always write down the unit with a measurement.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Measuring on a plan

subQuestions.label: 2.1.5 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
The actual outside length of the conference room is **12 m**. The outside length of the conference room measured on the layout plan is **12,7 cm** (127 mm).

Hence, calculate the scale used in this layout plan.

(Give the answer as a unit ratio in the form 1 : …)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Scale $= 12{,}7 \text{ cm} : 12 \text{ m}$ (1MCA correct order of the ratio — plan length first, real length second)
Mark 2: $= 12{,}7 : 1\,200$ (1C conversion of 12 m to 1 200 cm)
Mark 3: $= 1 : 94{,}49$ (1CA simplified unit ratio)

OR (using millimetres)

Mark 1: $125 \text{ mm} : 12 \text{ m}$ (1MCA correct order of the ratio)
Mark 2: $= 125 : 12\,000$ (1C conversion)
Mark 3: $= 1 : 96$ (1CA simplified unit ratio)

OR (papers measuring 12,4 cm)
$12{,}4 \text{ cm} : 12 \text{ m} = 12{,}4 : 1\,200 = 1 : 96{,}77$

OR (papers measuring 12,5 cm)
$12{,}5 \text{ cm} : 12 \text{ m} = 0{,}125 : 12 = 1 : 96$

NPR (no penalty for rounding)
Teaching point: A scale is always written *plan measurement : real measurement*, with BOTH values in the SAME unit and with no units shown. Divide both sides by the plan measurement to get the 1 : … form.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Calculating scale

subQuestions.questionText:
A single layer of the bottled water will be packed on a rectangular base. The packed bottled water will occupy **half of the length** of the rectangular refreshment table and will not overlap the edges of the table.

**DIMENSIONS OF THE RECTANGULAR REFRESHMENT TABLE TOP**

| Dimension | Measurement |
|---|---|
| Width | 49 cm |
| Length | 290 cm |

**PACKED BOTTLED WATER (rectangular base packaging)**

| Dimension | Measurement |
|---|---|
| Width | 24,2 cm |
| Length | 36,4 cm |

Calculate the maximum number of packed bottled water that can fit on this half of the table.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Half the table length $= 290 \text{ cm} \div 2 = 145 \text{ cm}$ (1A calculating half length)

**Packing the packs length-wise along the table's length:**
Mark 2: $\dfrac{145 \text{ cm}}{36{,}4 \text{ cm}} = 3{,}98$ (1MA dividing)
Mark 3: $\approx 3$ packs (1R rounding DOWN)

**And the pack width against the table width:**
Mark 4: $\dfrac{49 \text{ cm}}{24{,}2 \text{ cm}} = 2{,}02 = 2$ packs (1A simplification)

Mark 5: Number that can be packed $= 3 \times 2$ (1MA multiplying)
Mark 6: $= 6$ packs (1CA correct number of packs)

**But there is space left over:**
$36{,}4 \times 3 = 109{,}2 \text{ cm}$ and $145 \text{ cm} - 109{,}2 \text{ cm} = 35{,}8 \text{ cm}$ of table length is still free.
Packing width-wise into that strip: $\dfrac{35{,}8}{24{,}2} = 1{,}479\ldots \approx 1$ pack, and length against the width: $\dfrac{49}{36{,}4} = 1{,}346\ldots \approx 1$ pack.
Mark 7: 1 extra pack fits in the left-over strip (1A extra pack)

Mark 8: Total number of packs $= 6 + 1 = 7$ (1CA correct number of packs)

$\therefore$ The maximum is **7 packs**.

Teaching point: In packing questions you must ALWAYS round DOWN — 3,98 packs means only 3 whole packs fit. Then check the strip of table that is left over: turning the last pack sideways often lets one more pack fit, and that extra pack is worth a mark.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Packing and space arrangement

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE A is a road map with area information directing conference attendees to the Pretoria Hotel (marked 193 on the map). The map is NOT drawn to scale.

**Compass on the map:** the north arrow points to the LEFT of the map. So on this map north is to the left, east is towards the top, south is to the right and west is towards the bottom.

**Seven numbered approach routes are shown around the edge of the map:**

| Number | Approach route |
|---|---|
| 1 | N14 to Pretoria from Johannesburg |
| 2 | R21 to Pretoria from OR Tambo Int Airport |
| 3 | Rigel Avenue Off-ramp |
| 4 | Atterbury Road Off-ramp (off the N1 North to Polokwane) |
| 5 | Atterbury Road |
| 6 | N4 from Witbank |
| 7 | Church Street |

**Positions on the map:** Fountains Circle is drawn near the bottom of the map, towards the left of centre — routes 1 and 2 arrive at it from the right-hand edge. The Atterbury Road Off-ramp (route 4) is drawn near the top of the map, to the right of centre.

State the general direction of the Atterbury Road off-ramp from the Fountains Circle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **South East** OR **SE** (2A direction)
Teaching point: Always start at the place named after the word *from* (Fountains Circle) and look towards the other place. On this map north is to the LEFT, so east is towards the top and south is to the right. The off-ramp lies both towards the top (east) and towards the right (south) of Fountains Circle, giving south east.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Compass direction

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE A is a road map with area information directing conference attendees to the Pretoria Hotel. Printed in a block on the map, next to the north arrow, are the words:

> **Map is not drawn to scale.**

Explain the phrase, 'Map is not drawn to scale'.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: There is no relationship (no fixed ratio) between the distances on the map and the corresponding distances on the ground. (2A correct statement)

OR

Distances on the map are not accurate, therefore one should not measure a length on the document and then expect to be able to calculate the real-life distance from it. (2A correct statement)

OR

The map is a free-hand drawing / rough sketch, since no scale was used when it was drawn. (2A correct statement)

Teaching point: 'Not drawn to scale' does not mean the map is wrong — the streets are still in the right ORDER and the right relative position. It only means you may not measure the map with a ruler and convert to real distance.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Scale

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE A is a road map directing conference attendees to the Pretoria Hotel. The hotel is shown on the map by the black block marked **193**.

On the map, Kloof St runs across the map and ends where it meets Albert St, which runs at right angles to it. The block marked 193 is drawn in the corner formed where Kloof St meets Albert St. Tram St is the continuation of the same street further along, on the other side of Middle St.

Complete the following sentence:

Pretoria Hotel is at the corner of … and … Streets.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: **Kloof** Street (or **Tram** Street) (1RT reading Tram or Kloof from the map)
Mark 2: **Albert** Street (1RT reading Albert from the map)

So: Pretoria Hotel is at the corner of **Kloof Street and Albert Street**.

Teaching point: A building on a corner is named by the TWO streets that cross at that point. Find the marked block on the map, then read off the name of the street it faces and the name of the street that crosses it.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Locating a position

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE A is a road map directing conference attendees to the Pretoria Hotel.

The KEY of the map shows that a traffic light is drawn as a small black dot. Traffic lights (black dots) are drawn at several intersections on the map, for example in Church St, Middle St, Albert St and Eeufees St.

**Brooklyn Circle** is drawn on the map as a traffic circle (a small open circle where several roads meet). NO black dots are drawn at Brooklyn Circle.

State the probability of having a traffic light at Brooklyn Circle.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **0** (2A correct probability)

OR: Impossible / none / no chance / 0% (2A correct probability)

Teaching point: A probability of 0 means the event can never happen. Brooklyn Circle is a traffic *circle*, and the map shows no traffic-light dots there at all, so the probability of finding a traffic light there is zero.
subQuestions.topic: Probability – Impossible events

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE A is a road map directing conference attendees to the Pretoria Hotel.

Seven black circles numbered 1 to 7 are drawn around the edge of the map, each one at the point where a different road enters the map:

| Number | Road entering the map |
|---|---|
| 1 | N14 to Pretoria from Johannesburg |
| 2 | R21 to Pretoria from OR Tambo Int Airport |
| 3 | Rigel Avenue Off-ramp |
| 4 | Atterbury Road Off-ramp (off the N1 North to Polokwane) |
| 5 | Atterbury Road |
| 6 | N4 from Witbank |
| 7 | Church Street |

Give ONE reason why some streets are numbered from 1 to 7.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: They show the different roads / routes that lead to the hotel. (2O reason)

OR

The streets are the possible entry points for the conference attendees. (2O reason)

OR

It makes it easier to give directions to the destination. (2O reason)

Teaching point: Numbers like these on a directions map are route numbers, not house numbers. Each number marks one of the possible ways of arriving, so the hotel can simply tell a guest "follow route 4".
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Interpreting a road map

subQuestions.questionText:
A receptionist at the Pretoria Hotel has to report for work by 05:30.

She takes 10 minutes to walk from home to board a taxi.

- She leaves home at 04:55.
- She rides in a taxi for 20 minutes.
- She walks 5 minutes from the taxi stop to the hotel.

Verify whether or not the receptionist will get to work on time.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Arrival time $= 04{:}55 + 10 \text{ min} + 20 \text{ min} + 5 \text{ min}$ (1MA adding the time; 1A all the values)
Mark 3: $= 05{:}30$ (1CA arrival time)
Mark 4: The receptionist will be **on time** for work. (1O verification)

OR

Mark 1: Duration of the trip $= 10 \text{ min} + 20 \text{ min} + 5 \text{ min} = 35 \text{ min}$ (1A all the values)
Mark 2: Arrival time $= 04{:}55 + 00{:}35$ (1MA adding time)
Mark 3: $= 05{:}30$ (1CA arrival time)
Mark 4: She will be on time. (1O verification)

OR (working backwards)

Mark 1 & 2: $05{:}30 - 5 \text{ min} - 20 \text{ min} - 10 \text{ min}$ (1A all the values; 1MA subtracting time)
Mark 3: $= 04{:}55$ — exactly the time she leaves home (1CA departure time)
Mark 4: The receptionist will be on time for work. (1O verification)

Teaching point: With a "verify" question you must (i) show the calculation and (ii) write a clear conclusion sentence. She arrives at exactly 05:30, which is her reporting time, so she is on time — but with no minutes to spare.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Time calculations

questions.title: Fishing for carp, building a Vibracrete wall and painting the posts and post caps

subQuestions.questionText:
Andrew and Duncan went fishing for carp on a friend's farm.

NOTE: Carp is a large freshwater fish that can be eaten by humans.

A female carp can lay 2,7 million eggs.

Write 2,7 million in full, using numerals only.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Number of eggs $= 2{,}7 \times 1\,000\,000$ (1MA multiplying by 1 000 000)
Mark 2: $= 2\,700\,000$ (1A correct answer)

OR: Two million seven hundred thousand (answer only — full marks)

Teaching point: One million is 1 000 000 (a 1 followed by six zeros). To write 2,7 million in numerals, multiply 2,7 by 1 000 000, which moves the comma six places to the right.
subQuestions.topic: Number sense – Place value and large numbers

subQuestions.questionText:
Andrew and Duncan went fishing for carp on a friend's farm.

Andrew caught a carp with a mass of 2,375 kg. Duncan caught two carp, one weighing 1,2 kg and the other 750 g.

Determine, in kg, the total mass of the carp they caught.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Convert 750 g to kg: $\dfrac{750}{1\,000} = 0{,}75 \text{ kg}$ (1C conversion)
Mark 2: Total mass $= 2{,}375 \text{ kg} + 1{,}2 \text{ kg} + 0{,}75 \text{ kg}$ (1MA adding all the masses)
Mark 3: $= 4{,}325 \text{ kg}$ (1CA total mass in kg)

Teaching point: You may only add masses that are in the SAME unit. Convert grams to kilograms first by dividing by 1 000 ($1\,000 \text{ g} = 1 \text{ kg}$), then add.
subQuestions.topic: Conversions – Grams to kilograms

subQuestions.questionText:
Andrew wants to erect a Vibracrete wall on the boundary of his property.

- The wall will consist of concrete posts with precast concrete slabs between them.
- The wall will have **12 posts** planted into the ground using concrete.
- On top of each post, he will place a post cap.
- For each post, Andrew digs a **square hole** in the ground with a side length of **30 cm** and a depth of **60 cm**.

Calculate, in m³, the total capacity of all the holes dug for the required posts.

You may use the formula:

**Volume = length × width × depth**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Volume of ONE hole $= 30 \text{ cm} \times 30 \text{ cm} \times 60 \text{ cm}$ (1SF substitution into the formula)
Mark 2: $= 54\,000 \text{ cm}^3$ (1CA volume of the hole)
Mark 3 & 4: Total volume $= \dfrac{54\,000}{1\,000\,000} \text{ m}^3 \times 12$ (1C conversion factor $1 \text{ m}^3 = 1\,000\,000 \text{ cm}^3$; 1MA multiplying by 12 posts)
Mark 5: $= 0{,}648 \text{ m}^3$ (1CA simplification)

OR (convert first)

Mark 1 & 2: Volume $= 0{,}3 \text{ m} \times 0{,}3 \text{ m} \times 0{,}6 \text{ m}$ (1C conversion of cm to m; 1SF substitution)
Mark 3: $= 0{,}054 \text{ m}^3$ (1MA multiplying the converted values)
Mark 4: Total volume $= 0{,}054 \text{ m}^3 \times 12$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 5: $= 0{,}648 \text{ m}^3$ (1CA simplification for 12 posts)

OR

Total volume in m³ $= 12 \times (0{,}3 \times 0{,}3 \times 0{,}6) = 0{,}648$ (1MA multiply by 12 posts; 1C conversion; 1SF substitution; 1CA simplify bracket; 1CA simplification)

Teaching point: A square hole has equal length and width (30 cm by 30 cm), and the depth is the third dimension. The safest route is to convert the centimetres to metres FIRST — then the answer is already in m³ and you avoid the awkward $1\,000\,000$ conversion factor.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Volume of a rectangular prism

subQuestions.questionText:
Andrew is building a Vibracrete wall with 12 concrete posts. For each post he digs a square hole 30 cm × 30 cm and 60 cm deep. The total capacity of all 12 holes is 0,648 m³.

Andrew mixed the same volume of concrete as the volume calculated in QUESTION 3.2.1, that is 0,648 m³.

Give an explanation why he had some concrete left over after planting all the posts in the holes with concrete.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: The posts' volume will take up some of the volume of the concrete. (2O opinion)

OR

The posts will take up space in the hole. (2O opinion)

Teaching point: The hole is not filled with concrete alone — the post itself stands inside the hole and occupies part of that space. So the concrete actually needed is the hole volume MINUS the volume of the part of the post that is in the ground, which leaves some concrete over.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Volume in context

subQuestions.questionText:
The concrete for Andrew's Vibracrete wall is made from a mixture of cement, river sand and stone in the ratio illustrated below.

| Cement | River sand | Stone |
|---|---|---|
| 1 bag (50 kg) | 2 wheelbarrows | 2 wheelbarrows |

- 0,75 m³ of concrete requires 5,5 bags of cement.
- One level wheelbarrow full of river sand weighs 102 kg.

Calculate the mass of river sand needed to make 1 m³ of concrete.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: 5,5 bags of cement make 0,75 m³, so for 1 m³ the cement $= \dfrac{5{,}5}{0{,}75}$ (1MA working with the ratio)
Mark 2: $= 7{,}33\ldots$ bags (1A number of bags)

But 1 bag of cement is mixed with 2 wheelbarrows of sand.
Mark 3: Number of wheelbarrows of sand $= 7{,}333\ldots \times 2$ (1MA multiplying by 2)
Mark 4: $= 14{,}666\ldots$ wheelbarrows (1CA number of wheelbarrows)
Mark 5: Mass of the sand $= 102 \times 14{,}6666\ldots$ (1MA multiplying by the mass)
Mark 6: $= 1\,496 \text{ kg}$ (1CA simplification)

OR

Sand needed for 0,75 m³ of concrete $= 5{,}5 \times 2 = 11$ wheelbarrows (1MA working with the ratio; 1A number of wheelbarrows)
Mass of sand for 0,75 m³ $= 11 \times 102 \text{ kg} = 1\,122 \text{ kg}$ (1MCA multiplying by the mass; 1CA simplification)
Mass of sand for 1 m³ $= 1\,122 \text{ kg} \times \dfrac{1}{0{,}75} = 1\,496 \text{ kg}$ (1MA dividing by 0,75; 1CA simplification)

OR

For 0,75 m³: $5{,}5 \times 50 = 275 \text{ kg}$ cement; for 1 m³: $275 \div 0{,}75 = 366{,}666\ldots \text{ kg}$ cement (1MA dividing by 0,75; 1CA simplification)
Mixing ratio 1 bag : 2 wheelbarrows means cement 50 kg : 204 kg sand (1A mass of the wheelbarrows)
$366{,}66 : n \Rightarrow n = \dfrac{366{,}66}{50} \times 204 = 1\,496 \text{ kg}$ (1MCA multiplying by the mass; 1MA working with the ratio; 1CA simplification)

Teaching point: Work in two steps. First scale the CEMENT up from 0,75 m³ to 1 m³ (divide by 0,75). Then use the mixing ratio (1 bag needs 2 wheelbarrows) to turn bags into wheelbarrows, and finally multiply by 102 kg per wheelbarrow. Keep the full decimal 7,333… in your calculator — rounding early loses accuracy.
subQuestions.topic: Ratio and proportion – Mixing ratios

subQuestions.questionText:
Andrew's Vibracrete wall has **12 concrete posts**. Each post is **125 mm wide** and **1,6 m long**.

Andrew will paint **two sides of each of the concrete posts** (and all the outside faces of the post caps, which are dealt with separately).

The following formula may be used:

**Area of a rectangle = length × width**

Calculate, in cm², the total area of all the post sides that have to be painted.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Area of one rectangular side $= 1{,}6 \text{ m} \times 125 \text{ mm} = 160 \text{ cm} \times 12{,}5 \text{ cm}$ (1SF substitution; 1C converting both to cm)
$= 2\,000 \text{ cm}^2$
Mark 3: Total surface area $= 2\,000 \text{ cm}^2 \times 2 \text{ sides} \times 12 \text{ posts}$ (1MA multiplying by 2 and by 12)
Mark 4: $= 48\,000 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA simplification)

OR (work in metres and convert at the end)

Area $= 1{,}6 \text{ m} \times 0{,}125 \text{ m} = 0{,}2 \text{ m}^2$ (1SF substitution)
$0{,}2 \text{ m}^2 \times (2 \times 12) = 4{,}8 \text{ m}^2$ (1MA multiplying by 2 and 12)
$4{,}8 \text{ m}^2 \times 10\,000 = 48\,000 \text{ cm}^2$ (1C converting; 1CA simplification)

OR (work in millimetres)

Area $= 125 \text{ mm} \times 1\,600 \text{ mm} = 200\,000 \text{ mm}^2 = 2\,000 \text{ cm}^2$ (1SF substitution; 1C converting both)
Total $= 2\,000 \text{ cm}^2 \times 12 \times 2 = 48\,000 \text{ cm}^2$ (1MA multiply by 2 and 12; 1CA simplification)

Teaching point: The answer must be in cm², so convert BOTH measurements to centimetres before multiplying: $1{,}6 \text{ m} = 160 \text{ cm}$ and $125 \text{ mm} = 12{,}5 \text{ cm}$. Then remember two factors — 2 sides per post AND 12 posts.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Area of rectangles

subQuestions.questionText:
Andrew's Vibracrete wall has **12 concrete posts**, each with a post cap on top.

**The post cap:** it has a square base with a side length of **15,24 cm** and a constant (straight) side height of **2,5 cm**, with a pyramid-shaped top. The perpendicular height of each triangular face is **7,86 cm**.

The net of the faces of ONE post cap that have to be painted consists of:
- **4 rectangles**, each 15,24 cm long and 2,5 cm high, and
- **4 triangles**, each with a base of 15,24 cm and a perpendicular height of 7,86 cm.

**The posts:** the total area of all the post sides to be painted (2 sides on each of the 12 posts) is **48 000 cm²**.

The following formulae may be used:

**Area of a rectangle = length × width**

**Area of a triangle = ½ × base × perpendicular height**

Duncan stated that the total area of all the posts and the post caps to be painted was **52 704 cm²**, rounded to the nearest whole number.

Verify, showing ALL calculations, whether his statement is VALID.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Area of the rectangular part of one cap $= (15{,}24 \text{ cm} \times 2{,}5 \text{ cm}) \times 4$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 2: $= 38{,}1 \text{ cm}^2 \times 4 = 152{,}4 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA area of the 4 rectangles)

Mark 3 & 4: Area of the 4 top triangles $= \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \times 15{,}24 \text{ cm} \times 7{,}86 \text{ cm}\right) \times 4$ (1A multiplying by 4; 1SF substitution)
Mark 5: $= 59{,}8932 \text{ cm}^2 \times 4 = 239{,}5728 \text{ cm}^2$ (1CA simplification)

Total area of 1 post cap $= 152{,}4 \text{ cm}^2 + 239{,}5728 \text{ cm}^2 = 391{,}9728 \text{ cm}^2$

Mark 6: Total for the 12 caps and the posts $= 391{,}9728 \text{ cm}^2 \times 12 + 48\,000 \text{ cm}^2$ (1A multiplying by 12)
Mark 7: $= 4\,703{,}6736 + 48\,000 \approx 52\,704 \text{ cm}^2$ (1MCA adding the two areas)
Mark 8: The statement is **VALID**. (1O verification)

OR (single line of working)

Total area to be painted in cm²
$= (12 \times 4 \times 0{,}5 \times 15{,}24 \times 7{,}86) + (12 \times 4 \times 15{,}24 \times 2{,}5)$ (1A × 4; 1A × 12; 1SF; 1SF)
$= 2\,874{,}8736 + 1\,828{,}8$ (1CA triangle area; 1CA simplification)
$= 4\,703{,}6736 \approx 4\,704$
Posts + caps $= 48\,000 + 4\,704 = 52\,704$ (1MCA adding the two areas)
**VALID** (1O verification)

Teaching point: Work out ONE cap completely first (4 rectangles + 4 triangles), then multiply by 12, then add the 48 000 cm² of post sides. The bottom (square base) of the cap is NOT painted because it sits on top of the post. Finish with a clear word — VALID — or you lose the last mark.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Surface area of a composite object

subQuestions.questionText:
Andrew must paint a total area of **52 704 cm²** (the sides of the 12 concrete posts plus all the outside faces of the 12 post caps).

The spread rate of the paint is **12,46 litre/m²**.

Calculate how many litres of paint is needed to paint 52 704 cm².
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Area in m² $= 52\,704 \div 100^2 = 5{,}2704 \text{ m}^2$ (1C conversion)
Mark 2: Number of litres needed $= 5{,}2704 \times 12{,}46$ (1MCA multiplying)
Mark 3: $= 65{,}669\ldots \approx 66$ litres (1CA simplification; NPR)

Teaching point: The spread rate is given per SQUARE METRE, so the area must first be changed from cm² to m². Because $1 \text{ m} = 100 \text{ cm}$, we divide by $100^2 = 10\,000$ (not by 100). Round paint UP to a whole number of litres, since you cannot buy part of a litre.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Area conversion and spread rate

questions.title: Fashion show runways and seating layout, and a body type chart for dress sizes

subQuestions.questionText:
A programme inspiring people of all ages and genders usually ends with a fashion show.

ANNEXURE B shows the layout of the runways and the seating arrangements at the fashion show. The layout shows TWO runways:

| Runway | Length | Width |
|---|---|---|
| Floor runway | 54 feet (54') | 4 feet |
| Raised runway | 24 feet (24') | 4 feet |

NOTE: 54' means 54 feet. Each of the runways is 4 feet wide.

Write, in simplified form, the ratio of the width to the length of the raised runway.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: $4 : 24$ (1RT correct values; 1A correct order — width first, then length)
Mark 3: $= 1 : 6$ (1CA simplification; answer only earns full marks)

Teaching point: Write the two quantities down in the ORDER the question asks (width : length), then divide both parts by the highest common factor (4 here). Ratios have no units.
subQuestions.topic: Ratio – Simplifying ratios

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE B shows the layout of the runways at a fashion show:

| Runway | Length | Width |
|---|---|---|
| Floor runway | 54 feet (54') | 4 feet |
| Raised runway | 24 feet (24') | 4 feet |

NOTE: 1 m = 3,28084 feet

Convert the length of the floor runway to metres.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Length of runway $= \dfrac{54}{3{,}28084}$ (1RT correct runway length read from the layout; 1MA dividing by 3,28084)
Mark 3: $= 16{,}459199\ldots \text{ m}$ (1CA length of runway; NPR)

Teaching point: There are more feet than metres in the same distance, so the answer in metres must be SMALLER than 54 — that tells you to divide by 3,28084 and not to multiply.
subQuestions.topic: Conversions – Feet to metres

subQuestions.label: 4.1.3 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE B shows the seating arrangement at a fashion show. Next to the floor runway are single seats arranged in rows — THREE rows down each side of the floor runway.

On the layout the seats in the second and third rows are drawn slightly offset (staggered), so that each seat in the back rows sits in the gap between two seats of the row in front of it, instead of directly behind a seat.

Give a possible reason for the following:

Why the second- and third-row seats are not arranged exactly behind the first-row seats that are closest to the floor runway
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: To eliminate the obstruction that could be caused by the front-row spectators. (2O reason)

OR

To have a clear view of the models on the floor runway. (2O reason)

Teaching point: Staggering the seats means each person looks through the GAP between the two heads in front, instead of straight at the back of one head. This is the same reason cinema and stadium seats are staggered.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Interpreting a seating layout

subQuestions.label: 4.1.3 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE B shows the layout of the runways at a fashion show. There is a **floor runway** (54 feet long, at floor level) and a separate **raised runway** (24 feet long, built up higher than the floor). On the layout plan the two runways are drawn in line with one another, but with a clear open space (a gap) between the end of the one and the start of the other.

Give a possible reason for the following:

Why there is a gap between the two runways
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: The other runway is higher than the floor runway. (2O reason)

OR

It is a passage where people can pass through. (2O reason)

OR

There is a step between the two runways. (2O reason)

OR

To avoid collisions. (2O reason)

Teaching point: The two runways are at DIFFERENT heights, so the gap is where the step (or ramp) between them goes, and it also leaves a walkway for people and staff to cross between the seating areas.
subQuestions.topic: Maps and plans – Interpreting a layout plan

subQuestions.label: 4.1.4 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
At the fashion show there are 10 round tables next to the raised runway. Each round table can seat a maximum of 10 adults.

The diameter of the round table is **1,8288 m**.

You may use the following formula:

**Area of a circle = 3,142 × radius²**

Calculate the area of the top of ONE round table.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Radius $= \dfrac{1{,}8288 \text{ m}}{2} = 0{,}9144 \text{ m}$ (1A calculating the radius)
Mark 2: Area of a circle $= 3{,}142 \times (0{,}9144 \text{ m})^2$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 3: $= 2{,}627112\ldots \text{ m}^2$ (1CA area of circle; NPR)

Teaching point: The formula uses the RADIUS, but the question gives the DIAMETER. Always halve the diameter first — forgetting this step is the most common error in circle questions.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Area of a circle

subQuestions.label: 4.1.4 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
At the fashion show, each round table next to the raised runway can seat a maximum of **10 adults**. The diameter of the round table is **1,8288 m**.

Each person occupies an equal length of the outer edge around the round table.

You may use the following formula:

**Circumference of a circle = 3,142 × diameter**

Determine the maximum length allocated to each person seated around the round table.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Circumference $= 3{,}142 \times 1{,}8288 \text{ m}$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 2: $= 5{,}7460896 \text{ m}$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 3: Length allocated $= \dfrac{5{,}7460896 \text{ m}}{10}$ (1MCA dividing by 10)
Mark 4: $= 0{,}5746\ldots \text{ m}$ (1CA length per person; NPR)

Teaching point: "Around the outer edge" means the CIRCUMFERENCE (the distance right around the circle), not the area. Because the 10 people are spaced equally, simply divide the circumference by 10.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Circumference of a circle

subQuestions.questionText:
The girls participating in the fashion show need dresses that fit well. ANNEXURE C shows a body type chart used to select the correct dress size.

**TABLE 1: BODY TYPE CHART USED TO SELECT DRESS SIZE**

| Height ↓ / Mass → | 50 kg | 55 kg | 60 kg | 65 kg | 67 kg | 70 kg | 75 kg | 80 kg | 85 kg | 90 kg | 100 kg |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,50 m | XS | S | S | M | L | L | XL | XL | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,55 m | XS | XS | S | M | M | L | L | XL | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,60 m | XS | XS | S | S | M | L | L | L | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,65 m | XS | XS | S | S | M | L | L | L | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,70 m | XS | XS | S | S | M | M | L | L | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,75 m | XS | XS | XS | S | S | M | M | L | XL | XL | XXL |
| **Dress size** | 0–2 | 2–4 | 4–6 | 6–8 | 8–10 | 10–12 | 12–14 | 14–16 | 16–18 | 18–20 | 20–22 |
| **Body size** | XS | XS | S | S | M | M | M | L | L | XL | XXL |

Write down the body size for a girl with a mass of 55 kg and a height of 1,6 m.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **XS** (2RT correct size)

Teaching point: Read across from the 1,60 m row and down from the 55 kg column — the cell where they meet gives the body size. Take care to use the row for the correct height; the 1,50 m row would have given S instead.
subQuestions.topic: Data handling – Reading a two-way table

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE C shows a body type chart used to select the correct dress size at the fashion show.

**TABLE 1: BODY TYPE CHART USED TO SELECT DRESS SIZE**

| Height ↓ / Mass → | 50 kg | 55 kg | 60 kg | 65 kg | 67 kg | 70 kg | 75 kg | 80 kg | 85 kg | 90 kg | 100 kg |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,50 m | XS | S | S | M | L | L | XL | XL | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,55 m | XS | XS | S | M | M | L | L | XL | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,60 m | XS | XS | S | S | M | L | L | L | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,65 m | XS | XS | S | S | M | L | L | L | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,70 m | XS | XS | S | S | M | M | L | L | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,75 m | XS | XS | XS | S | S | M | M | L | XL | XL | XXL |
| **Dress size** | 0–2 | 2–4 | 4–6 | 6–8 | 8–10 | 10–12 | 12–14 | 14–16 | 16–18 | 18–20 | 20–22 |
| **Body size** | XS | XS | S | S | M | M | M | L | L | XL | XXL |

State the mass of a girl with a height of 1,75 m wearing dress size 14–16.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **80 kg** (2RT correct weight)

Teaching point: This is a backwards reading. Find the dress size 14–16 in the bottom rows, go straight up that column to the mass heading (80 kg) and check that the 1,75 m row in that column agrees (it shows L, which matches dress size 14–16).
subQuestions.topic: Data handling – Reading a two-way table

subQuestions.questionText:
The girls participating in the fashion show need dresses that fit well.

Calculate the body mass index (BMI) of a girl who weighs 70 kg and is 1,50 m tall.

You may use the formula:

$$\text{BMI} = \dfrac{\text{mass (kg)}}{(\text{height in metres})^2}$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: $\text{BMI} = \dfrac{70 \text{ kg}}{(1{,}50 \text{ m})^2}$ (1MA correct numerator; 1MA correct denominator)
Mark 3: $= 31{,}11\ldots \text{ kg/m}^2$ (1A correct BMI; NPR)

Teaching point: The height must be SQUARED before you divide: $(1{,}50)^2 = 2{,}25$, so $\text{BMI} = 70 \div 2{,}25 = 31{,}11\ldots$. On your calculator, put the whole denominator in brackets.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – BMI calculation

subQuestions.questionText:
The fashion show uses an **equal number** of girls for each size. The body type chart below is used to select the correct dress size.

**TABLE 1: BODY TYPE CHART USED TO SELECT DRESS SIZE**

| Height ↓ / Mass → | 50 kg | 55 kg | 60 kg | 65 kg | 67 kg | 70 kg | 75 kg | 80 kg | 85 kg | 90 kg | 100 kg |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,50 m | XS | S | S | M | L | L | XL | XL | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,55 m | XS | XS | S | M | M | L | L | XL | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,60 m | XS | XS | S | S | M | L | L | L | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,65 m | XS | XS | S | S | M | L | L | L | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,70 m | XS | XS | S | S | M | M | L | L | XL | XL | XXL |
| 1,75 m | XS | XS | XS | S | S | M | M | L | XL | XL | XXL |

Write, as a percentage, the probability of randomly selecting a girl who weighs 50 kg and wears an XS dress.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: **100%** (2A correct probability)

Teaching point: Look down the whole 50 kg column: every single cell — for every height from 1,50 m to 1,75 m — shows XS. So a girl of 50 kg is CERTAIN to wear XS, and a certain event has a probability of 1, that is 100%.
subQuestions.topic: Probability – Certain events

subQuestions.questionText:
The fashion show uses an **equal number** of girls for each size.

The body type chart uses the following body sizes, from smallest to largest:

**XS, S, M, L, XL, XXL**

Bonolo stated that the probability of randomly selecting a girl wearing a dress with body size smaller than XXL is 0,833.

Verify, with calculations, whether her statement is VALID.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: $\text{P(smaller than XXL)} = \dfrac{5}{6}$ (1A numerator — the 5 sizes XS, S, M, L and XL; 1A denominator — the 6 possible body sizes)
Mark 3: $= 0{,}833$ (1CA simplification)
Mark 4: The statement is **VALID**. (1O opinion)

Teaching point: Because an equal number of girls wears each size, each of the 6 body sizes is equally likely. Five of those six sizes (XS, S, M, L, XL) are smaller than XXL, giving $\frac{5}{6} = 0{,}8333\ldots \approx 0{,}833$. Remember to finish with the word VALID — the conclusion carries a mark.
subQuestions.topic: Probability – Calculating and verifying a probability

questions.title: Ice cubes and ice hotels, and shipping distances between Anchorage and world cities

subQuestions.questionText:
Ice is usually used in cool drinks to further cool them. Ice can be made by freezing water in different shapes. Cubes are the most common shape used to make ice.

The **side length of the ice cube is 4,5 cm**.

Determine the surface area of a cube.

You may use the formula:

**Surface area of a cube = 6 × side length²**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Surface area of a cube $= 6 \times (4{,}5 \text{ cm})^2$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 2 & 3: $= 121{,}5 \text{ cm}^2$ (1A simplification; 1A unit; answer only earns full marks)

Teaching point: A cube has 6 identical square faces, which is where the 6 in the formula comes from. Square the side length first: $(4{,}5)^2 = 20{,}25$, then multiply by 6. Because it is an AREA, the unit must be cm² — leaving off the squared unit costs a mark here.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Surface area of a cube

subQuestions.questionText:
Countries surrounding the North Pole have started building ice hotels for travellers to stay overnight. The hotel buildings, with furniture and decorations, are made of big blocks of ice, **each weighing two tons**. Blocks of ice are stacked on top of each other to build a room.

Calculate the total mass (in kg) of a wall built with **60 big blocks of ice**.

NOTE: 1 kg = 0,001 ton
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Total mass $= 60 \times 2 \text{ ton} = 120 \text{ ton}$ (1MA multiplying by 2; 1A simplification)
Mark 3: $= \dfrac{120}{0{,}001} \text{ kg}$ (1C conversion)
Mark 4: $= 120\,000 \text{ kg}$ (1CA simplification)

OR

Mark 1: $1 \text{ ton} = 1\,000 \text{ kg}$ (1C conversion)
Mark 2 & 3: $1\,000 \text{ kg} \times 2 = 2\,000 \text{ kg}$ per block (1MA multiplying by 2; 1A simplification)
Mark 4: Mass of 60 blocks $= 2\,000 \times 60 = 120\,000 \text{ kg}$ (1CA simplification)

Teaching point: Do the two jobs one at a time — first the total in tons ($60 \times 2 = 120$ ton), then the conversion to kilograms. Since $1 \text{ kg} = 0{,}001 \text{ ton}$, one ton is 1 000 kg, so tons $\to$ kg means multiply by 1 000 (or divide by 0,001).
subQuestions.topic: Conversions – Tons to kilograms

subQuestions.questionText:
At an ice hotel, ice can be carved to form different shapes.

A block of ice was carved out to make a circular opening. The carved-out ice was melted, resulting in water with a volume of **38 500 cm³**.

Calculate the volume of the ice that was carved out.

You may use the formula:

**Volume of water = volume of ice × 0,92**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: $38\,500 \text{ cm}^3 = \text{volume of ice} \times 0{,}92$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 2: $\dfrac{38\,500}{0{,}92} \text{ cm}^3 = \text{volume of ice}$ (1MA changing the subject of the formula)
Mark 3: $41\,847{,}826\ldots \text{ cm}^3 = $ volume of ice (1A volume of ice; NPR)

Teaching point: The water volume is given and the ICE volume is unknown, so you must work backwards through the formula — divide by 0,92 instead of multiplying. Check your answer for sense: ice takes up more space than the water it melts into, so the ice volume must be BIGGER than 38 500 cm³.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Volume and changing the subject of a formula

subQuestions.questionText:
Alaska is one of the states in the USA. Anchorage is the largest city in Alaska. ANNEXURE D shows a part of the globe indicating the shortest distances, in nautical miles, between Anchorage and a few selected cities in the world.

The distances labelled on the globe are:

| Route | Distance (nautical miles) |
|---|---|
| Anchorage – Berlin | 3 950 |
| Anchorage – Moscow | 3 800 |
| Anchorage – Beijing | 3 475 |
| Anchorage – Seoul | 3 300 |
| Anchorage – Washington | 2 900 |
| Anchorage – Los Angeles | 2 000 |
| Los Angeles – Honolulu | 2 607 |
| Tokyo – Honolulu | 3 350 |

(One further route on the far eastern side of the globe is labelled 3 625; its city falls outside the part of the globe that is shown.)

Determine, in nautical miles, the difference in the distances from Tokyo to Honolulu and from Washington to Anchorage.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Difference $= 3\,350 - 2\,900$ (1RT 1st value; 1RT 2nd value)
Mark 3: $= 450$ nautical miles (1CA with subtraction; NPU; answer only earns full marks)

Teaching point: "Difference" means subtract, always taking the smaller value away from the larger one so that the answer is positive. Write the unit (nautical miles) with your answer.
subQuestions.topic: Data handling – Reading values and finding a difference

subQuestions.questionText:
ANNEXURE D shows a part of the globe indicating the shortest distances, in nautical miles, between Anchorage and a few selected cities in the world. The **distance from Berlin to Anchorage is 3 950 nautical miles**.

NOTE:
- 1 nautical mile = 1,151 miles
- 1 km = 0,6215 miles

Convert, to kilometres, the distance from Berlin to Anchorage.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 & 2: Distance in miles $= 3\,950 \times 1{,}151$ (1RT value of 3 950; 1C multiplying by 1,151)
$= 4\,546{,}45$ miles
Mark 3: Distance in km $= \dfrac{4\,546{,}45}{0{,}6215}$ (1C dividing by 0,6215)
Mark 4: $= 7\,315{,}285599 \text{ km}$ (1CA simplification)

OR (one step)

Distance in km $= 3\,950 \times \dfrac{1{,}151}{0{,}6215} = 7\,315{,}285599 \text{ km}$ (1RT value of 3 950; 1C multiply by 1,151; 1C divide by 0,6215; 1CA simplification; NPR)

Teaching point: This is a two-step conversion: nautical miles $\to$ miles $\to$ kilometres. Because $1 \text{ km} = 0{,}6215$ miles, there are MORE kilometres than miles in the same distance, so the last step is a division by 0,6215.
subQuestions.topic: Conversions – Nautical miles, miles and kilometres

subQuestions.label: 5.3.3 (a)
subQuestions.questionText:
Cargo needs to be shipped from Los Angeles to Honolulu and then from Honolulu to Tokyo.

Phenyo searched the internet to determine how long it would take the cargo to reach its destination. Shown below are the search results. Some information has been omitted.

| Ocean route | Time | Distance |
|---|---|---|
| USLAX Los Angeles → USHNL Honolulu | 10 days 4 hours | 2 607 nautical miles |
| USHNL Honolulu → JPYOK Tokyo | … | 3 350 nautical miles |

NOTE: Ships sail 24 hours a day.

Calculate the average speed of the ship, rounded to TWO decimal places, in nautical miles per hour.

You may use the formula: **Distance = speed × time**
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: 10 days 4 hours $= (10 \times 24) + 4 = 244$ hours (1C conversion)
Mark 2: $2\,607 = \text{speed} \times 244 \text{ hours}$ (1SF substitution)
Mark 3: $\dfrac{2\,607}{244} = \text{speed}$ (1MA changing the subject of the formula)
Mark 4: Average speed $\approx 10{,}68$ nautical miles/hour (1R simplification correctly rounded)

OR

10 days 4 hours $= 244$ hours (1C conversion)
Hours for the second part $= \dfrac{3\,350 \times 244}{2\,607} = 313{,}54$ hours
$\text{Average speed} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{3\,350 + 2\,607}{313{,}54 + 244} = \dfrac{5\,957}{557{,}54} = 10{,}68$ nautical miles/hour (1MA changing the subject; 1SF substitution; 1R correctly rounded)

Teaching point: Time must be in HOURS before you divide, because the answer is asked for in nautical miles per hour. Ships sail 24 hours a day, so 10 days = 240 hours, plus 4 hours = 244 hours.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Average speed

subQuestions.label: 5.3.3 (b)
subQuestions.questionText:
Cargo is shipped from Los Angeles to Honolulu and then from Honolulu to Tokyo.

| Ocean route | Time | Distance |
|---|---|---|
| USLAX Los Angeles → USHNL Honolulu | 10 days 4 hours | 2 607 nautical miles |
| USHNL Honolulu → JPYOK Tokyo | … | 3 350 nautical miles |

NOTE: Ships sail 24 hours a day.

The average speed of the ship is **10,68 nautical miles per hour**.

Hence, determine the date and time of arrival in Tokyo if the ship leaves Honolulu on **24 September at 16:00** and sails at the same average speed.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Time $= \dfrac{3\,350 \text{ miles}}{10{,}68 \text{ nautical miles/hour}}$ (1MA dividing by the speed)
Mark 2: $= 313{,}67$ hours (1CA hours)
Mark 3: $= \dfrac{313{,}67 \text{ hours}}{24 \text{ hours}}$ (1C conversion to days)
Mark 4 & 5: $= 13$ days and 1,67 hours (1CA number of days; 1CA hours)
Mark 6: Arrival date and time: **7 October at 17:40** (1CA correct date and time)

OR (using the ratio, without rounding the speed)

Ship travels 2 607 in 244 hours, and 3 350 in $n$ hours:
$n = \dfrac{3\,350 \times 244}{2\,607} = 313{,}5404679708$ hours (1MA using the ratio; 1CA hours)
$313{,}5404679708 \div 24 = 13{,}064186$ (1C conversion)
$= 13$ days and 1,54 hours $= 13$ days 1 hour 32 min (1CA number of days; 1CA hours)
Arrive **7 October at 17:32** (1CA correct date and time)

Teaching point: Convert the decimal part of the day into hours and minutes: 0,67 of an hour is $0{,}67 \times 60 \approx 40$ minutes. Then count the days forward carefully — 24 September plus 13 days lands on 7 October (September has 30 days), and 16:00 plus 1 h 40 min gives 17:40.
subQuestions.topic: Measurement – Time, distance and speed
